title: Is this patient note safe to file?
prompt:
Create a large 16:9 landscape infographic for a general professional audience (managers, engineers new to the topic, students), light near-white background, warm and clear like a well-designed museum explainer or a quality newspaper graphic. Plain everyday language is the main text; technical names appear only as small grey secondary labels.

TITLE (large): "Is this patient note safe to file?"
SUBTITLE: "TOKN checked six synthetic emergency-department cases for private data and valid diagnosis codes before they entered the record."

BAND 1 — heading "Why this matters": one wide card with a simple flat illustration of a hospital clipboard with a padlock, and this text: "A hospital record must never leak a patient's identifiers, and every diagnosis code must be valid: mistakes follow a patient for years."

BAND 2 — heading "Who did the work": a left-to-right flow of eight round role badges joined by arrows. Each badge shows a line icon, the bold role name, the short description in quotes, and the model name tiny and grey below:
1 Scout — "lists the tools available" (claude-haiku-5.5) [icon: binoculars]
2 Planner — "writes what 'done' looks like" (claude-opus-5.5) [icon: document]
3 Analyst — "runs the official checks" (Kimi-K3.1-Pro) [icon: bar chart]
4 Skeptic — "re-checks and finds 5 weak spots" (FW-GLM-5.3) [icon: shield]
5 Judge — "decides: revise or ship?" (Microsoft-Decision-1) [icon: balance scale]
6 Editor — "fixes every weak spot" (gpt-6.1-sol) [icon: pencil]
7 Coach — "writes a lesson for next time" (claude-opus-5.5) [icon: lightbulb]
8 Examiner — "scores it with plain code, no AI" (verify.py) [icon: checklist]
Caption under the flow: "Like a newsroom: a writer, a fact-checker, an editor — and an exam nobody can sweet-talk."

BAND 3 — heading "Four questions every case must answer": four cards in a row, each with an icon, the question in large plain words, and a tiny grey tool label:
(siren icon) "How urgent is the case?" — tiny grey label: ed_triage
(padlock icon) "Does the note contain private identifiers?" — tiny grey label: ed_phi_attest
(code tag icon) "Is the diagnosis code valid?" — tiny grey label: ed_diagnosis_record
(stethoscope icon) "Is it ready for clinician review?" — tiny grey label: ed_clinician_review

BAND 4 — heading "What it found": 6 result cards in a row. Each shows the small ID at top, a large verdict word in its color with a matching status icon, and one plain sentence:
ED-01 — green (#16A34A) verdict "Accepted" — "Chest pain, valid code I21.4."
ED-02 — red (#DC2626) verdict "Blocked: private data" — "Note contains a medical record number."
ED-03 — green (#16A34A) verdict "Accepted" — "A reagent lot number is not a social security number."
ED-04 — amber (#D97706) verdict "Code sent back" — "Diagnosis code in the wrong format."
ED-05 — amber (#D97706) verdict "Code sent back" — "Diagnosis code in the wrong format."
ED-06 — red (#DC2626) verdict "Blocked: private data" — "Note contains an email address."
Small note at the right of the heading: "Private data is blocked before anything else is recorded."

BOTTOM BAND — three short panels:
"Trust, but verify" — "An independent checker re-ran the checks and plain code graded the result: 6 of 6 correct."
"Honest wording" — "It supports intake; a clinician still reviews every case."
"Getting better each run" — "The lesson saved for next time: Keep each check's exact input and output in the result, so reviewers verify from the record."

FOOTER (small, centered): "The takeaway: Blocking a real leak matters. So does not blocking a harmless number."

TEXT DISCIPLINE: use ONLY the words given above in quotes plus the headings. Do NOT add any slogans, taglines, mottos, handwritten notes, brand lines, decorative words, extra footers or invented statistics. Every word spelled exactly as given and legible at 4K.

Visual rules: generous whitespace, strong hierarchy (title > band headings > plain sentences > tiny grey technical labels), verdict colors only on the result cards, soft blue/teal section tints, flat friendly line icons. No people, no faces, no photos.
